summary: SIP back-to-back user agents can cause endless request loops because they generate new requests with fresh Max-Forwards values. This document discusses why loop detection is difficult for these devices and sets out requirements for them to prevent infinite loops.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP back-to-back user agent can create a new request and accidentally keep a routing loop going. This RFC requires it to carry forward the request's hop limit and parallel-request limit so the loop cannot grow without bound.

questions: why do sip loops happen with b2bua
how does a b2bua prevent sip loops
subtitle: B2BUAs must preserve SIP hop and breadth limits when they create new requests.

tldr.problem: A back-to-back user agent can create a new SIP request with a fresh Max-Forwards value, allowing a misconfigured routing loop to continue without a useful hop limit.
tldr.mechanism: B2BUAs must copy and decrement Max-Forwards, and must copy and handle Max-Breadth as a proxy would. Via-based loop detection is recommended.
tldr.outcome: The rules bound loops and preserve parallel-forking limits; privacy choices that hide hop counts can conflict with them.

today: RFC 7332 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Loops Can Continue
sections.content:
SIP uses Max-Forwards to limit how many network hops a request can take. A back-to-back user agent (B2BUA) acts as a user agent server on one side and a user agent client on the other, so it can create a new request instead of forwarding the old one.

Some B2BUAs reset Max-Forwards in the new request. This can make a misconfiguration loop unbounded. Via-based detection can also be delayed when the B2BUA does not copy Via fields.
sections.plainLanguage: A B2BUA can create a fresh request instead of passing the received one along. If it resets the hop limit, requests can keep circling through a misconfigured network.

sections.title: Loop Detection and Max-Forwards
sections.content:
B2BUAs are RECOMMENDED to implement the Via loop-detection mechanism defined for proxies in RFC 5393. For dialog-forming and out-of-dialog requests, every B2BUA MUST copy the received Max-Forwards value and decrement it as a proxy would.

A B2BUA MUST reject or respond to a request whose received value is zero. If the request has no Max-Forwards field, the B2BUA MUST add one; its value SHOULD be 70. Applying this behavior to in-dialog requests is optional and may cause issues for some devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Each B2BUA must carry the hop countdown into its new request and reduce it. If there is no countdown, it should start at 70; a request at zero must not continue.

sections.title: The Max-Breadth Limit
sections.content:
Max-Breadth limits parallel forking, where one request produces several parallel requests. Every B2BUA MUST copy the received Max-Breadth field and follow the proxy rules in RFC 5393, including creating the field when absent and limiting its maximum value.

A B2BUA that generates parallel requests for one incoming request MUST handle Max-Breadth as a parallel-forking proxy would.
sections.plainLanguage: Max-Breadth limits how many parallel requests can be made. A B2BUA must preserve and apply that limit when it creates requests.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no security issues beyond those in RFC 5393. Some B2BUAs reset Max-Forwards and Max-Breadth to hide how many hops a request has crossed, for privacy or security reasons.

That goal conflicts with the loop protections here. Manufacturers MUST use the specified behavior by default, but MAY offer user-configurable overrides.
sections.plainLanguage: Hiding hop counts can conflict with stopping loops. The specified protections must be the default, though an administrator may be given an override.
